Grade 2 · Unit 2-B

Plants, Animals, and Habitats

How do plants, animals, and homes depend on each other?

Plants and animals depend on each other and on the places they live. You will test what plants need by changing one thing at a time, see how animals carry seeds and pollen, and compare how different habitats support different kinds of living things.

In this lesson

  1. Do plants need sunlight and water?
  2. Animals move seeds and pollen
  3. Different habitats have different living things
  4. Try it at home
  5. Check yourself
  6. Play: Plants, Animals, and Habitats

You did this before / what is new. You observed plant needs and habitats in K-C; now you run a longer bean investigation and compare habitats with numbers.

Concept 1

Do plants need sunlight and water?

Plants need sunlight and water to grow; we can test one thing at a time.

Try it

Grow bean plants in cups: sun + water, dark + water, sun + no water. Use pre-grown plants or the provided dataset if time is short (the dataset is only for analyzing provided data).

“Which bean grew?”

You did this before / what is new: In K-C you noticed that plants need sunlight and water; now you test that yourself, with three conditions (sun + water, dark + water, sun + no water) and height measured in paper clips on day 7 and day 14. One messy cup is not the finding: grow more than one cup for each condition, repeat the test the same way, and compare before you decide.

Data

Picture graph or simple bar graph of plant heights.

“Light plants were green and sturdy. Dark plants were pale and thin.” Dark plants can stretch tall, but they are weak.

Real world

Michigan farms grow corn, apples, and beans using sunlight and water.

“Corn uses sunlight and water.”

Concept 2

Animals move seeds and pollen

Animals carry seeds and move pollen; these interactions help plants make new plants, and animals often get food from plants.

Analogy

An animal can be like a delivery helper. The bee = the delivery helper. Pollen = the package, delivered flower to flower. A bird carries seeds in its tummy or on its feet and drops them far away.

Where it breaks: bees and birds are not trying to deliver. They are just looking for food.

“A bee carries pollen. A bird carries seeds.”

Diagram

Flower → bee → flower; berry → bird → new place.

“Pollen moves. Seeds move. The bee gets nectar. The bird gets a berry.”

Try it

Guess first: Will your pipe-cleaner bee move the yellow powder from one paper flower to another?

What you need: two or three paper flowers, a pipe cleaner “bee”, yellow cornmeal or flour (pollen), a fuzzy sock, felt, burrs or Velcro dots.

Do: Sprinkle a little yellow powder in one flower. Touch the bee to it, then touch the bee to the next flower. Or, wear a fuzzy sock on a short walk through tall grass and see what sticks.

Look for: Did powder move to the second flower? Did seeds or hooks stick to the sock?

What it shows: Animals carry pollen and seeds without knowing it, and that helps plants make new plants.

Safety: Do not taste the powder, seeds, or berries. Wash hands after.

“Make a model. Move the powder.”

Data

Model test chart.

“Hooks stuck. Powder moved.”

Concept 3

Different habitats have different living things

Different habitats have different kinds and numbers of plants and animals.

Diagram

Pond, forest, and sand dune.

“A pond gives fish water.”

Try it

Sort Michigan plants and animals into habitats.

“Where does the frog live?”

Data

Compare two habitats by counting the kinds of living things you really find in a same-size patch of each, in the same amount of time (picture cards are a backup).

“In our patch, the forest had __ kinds and the dune had __ kinds.”

Real world

Great Lakes shores have water, sand, plants, birds, and insects.

“The shore is a home.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Seed or Pollen Mover Model. Problem: a plant needs help moving pollen or seeds. Students build a paper seed with hooks or a pipe-cleaner “bee,” test it 3 times on felt/fuzz or paper flowers, and record whether pollen or seeds moved. Criteria: moves or sticks in at least 2 of 3 tries. Constraints: use kit materials.

Try it

What you need

bean seeds, cups, soil or paper towels, water, sunny spot, dark box or cupboard, fuzz sock or felt, burrs or Velcro dots, paper flowers, pipe cleaners, yellow cornmeal or flour, Michigan habitat picture cards, tally paper, crayons.

Safety: Wash hands after soil, seeds, and outdoor materials. No tasting seeds, berries, or powder. No coin cells or magnets are required.

Try it

What you do

1. Bean test (a few minutes a day for 2 weeks). Grow beans in sun with water, dark with water, and sun with no water. Measure height in paper clips on day 7 and day 14.

2. Seed or pollen mover (25 minutes). Build a hooked paper seed or a pipe-cleaner bee. Test it 3 times and tally how many times it moved or stuck.

3. Habitat counts (20 minutes). Count the kinds of living things in a same-size patch of two habitats, for the same time.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but the standard expects you to collect your own when you can.

Real observation log is preferred. If plants or outdoor observations are not possible, this dataset is a partial path: analysis of provided data for 2-LS2-1 and 2-LS4-1. With the backup you do not plan, conduct, or observe anything: you read the tables, compare conditions or habitats, and explain what the numbers show. The full path is your own bean-test log and your own habitat counts; the backup only covers the compare-and-explain part. What is new here: sun and water are changed one at a time, and plants are checked at day 7 and day 14. Use two or more plants per condition, and judge by leaves and color, not height alone. A plant in the dark can grow tall but stay pale and thin (see 3.3 and 5.3), so one height number from one plant can mislead. Check yourself

What did you learn?

0 of 4 correct

Words to know

sunlight
light from the Sun.
water
liquid plants and animals need.
grow
get bigger or change over time.
seed
plant part that can grow into a new plant.
pollen
tiny powder that helps some plants make seeds.
pollinate
move pollen to help a plant make seeds.
disperse
spread or carry seeds.
habitat
a home that gives living things what they need.
diversity
many different kinds.
model
a simple way to show how something works.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Plants eat soil.” Correct: plants use sunlight, water, and air to grow; soil gives water and minerals.
  • “Animals do not need plants.” Correct: animals depend on plants for food, shelter, and many interactions.
  • “A habitat is only where an animal sleeps.” Correct: a habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space.
  • “Seeds only fall straight down.” Correct: animals, wind, and water can move seeds.
  • “Bees only make honey.” Correct: bees also move pollen, which helps flowers make seeds and fruit.

Limits and cautions:

  • Bean plants need days to weeks; start two weeks early. If you use the provided dataset, that is a partial path: students analyze provided data, they do not plan or conduct the test.
  • Outdoor seed walks need safe spaces; use felt or indoor burrs if needed.
  • Use cornmeal or flour instead of real pollen if allergies are a concern.
  • Wash hands after soil and outdoor materials.
  • If an extension uses lights or magnets, use ready-made lamps only and keep magnets away from Chromebooks.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • 2-LS2-1: Plan and conduct an investigation to determine if plants need sunlight and water to grow. Full path: students plan and run the bean test themselves. Partial path: the provided bean dataset, where students only analyze provided data (compare and explain) and do not plan or conduct.
  • 2-LS2-2: Develop a simple model that mimics the function of an animal in dispersing seeds or pollinating plants.
  • 2-LS4-1: Make observations of plants and animals to compare the diversity of life in different habitats.

Connections: - Builds on: K-C *Living Things and Their Homes*; K-B *Sunlight, Weather, and Staying Safe*; 1-B *Parts, Parents, and Young*. - Builds toward: 3.3 *Life Cycles and Traits*; 3.4 *Survival, Fossils, and Change*; 5.3 *Energy and Matter in Ecosystems*; Unit 8: *Classifying Life*; Unit 12: *Ecosystems & Food Webs*; 7.5 *Photosynthesis & Matter Cycling*.
